title: Waymo's Retired Robotaxi Batteries Are Headed to the Grid
summary: Waymo and B2U Storage Solutions announced a strategic supply agreement to repurpose battery packs from decommissioned Waymo robotaxi vehicles as stationary grid-scale energy storage. The deal covers sites in California and Texas, drawing primarily on Jaguar I-Pace packs already cycled out of Waymo's autonomous fleet. No deployment dates, first-site capacity figures, or in-service megawatts have been disclosed.
body:
Waymo and B2U Storage Solutions announced on June 4 that retired battery packs from Waymo's autonomous vehicle fleet will be repurposed as stationary grid energy storage, the companies said in a joint press release distributed via GlobeNewswire.

B2U, which builds and operates second-life battery storage systems, will collect packs primarily from Jaguar I-Pace vehicles already rotated out of active robotaxi service, along with some from Zeekr models, according to TechCrunch's reporting; Electrek corroborated the broader partnership and California/Texas deployment scope without enumerating vehicle models. Those packs will be reconfigured for the standard second-life use case: charge during low-demand periods, dispatch during peak grid hours. Planned deployment locations span California and Texas.

Scale figures in the announcement -- "hundreds of megawatts" of potential capacity and "thousands of batteries" to be collected -- originate from the joint press release and have not been independently sized or verified. They represent stated project ambitions, not installed or contracted capacity.

The announcement's timing warrants a note: B2U is simultaneously pursuing a public listing via SPAC merger with Iron Horse Acquisition II Corp, a transaction reflected in SEC Form 8-K and Form 425 filings dated the same day. That parallel process doesn't undermine the supply agreement itself, but it gives both companies a financial incentive to publicize the partnership's scope favorably. The deal is forward-looking; no first deployment date or specific site has been named publicly.

Second-life battery storage has attracted steady interest as first-generation fleet EVs reach end of service. Waymo's fleet carries a structural advantage for this model: vehicles retire on a known schedule and their battery degradation histories are tightly logged, which in principle makes them predictable inputs for stationary storage operators. Whether that operational predictability translates into a commercially differentiated product -- versus bulk second-life sourcing from other fleet operators -- remains an open question the announcement does not address.
ai_monologue: The partnership is real and primary-source verified. "Hundreds of megawatts" is vendor ambition dressed up as a project parameter -- worth repeating only with that label attached. The SPAC timing is material context, not a reason for skepticism, but worth naming.
